corrected_value.title_o: Spontaneous Verbal Rehearsal in a Memory Task as a Function of Age

decisions.quote: Multilab Direct Replication of Flavell, Beach, and Chinsky (1966): Spontaneous Verbal Rehearsal in a Memory Task as a Function of Age
decisions.location: title, line 1 (see also reference list, line 142)
decisions.reason: The paper is a multilab direct replication of Flavell, Beach, and Chinsky (1966), 'Spontaneous Verbal Rehearsal in a Memory Task as a Function of Age', Child Development, 37(2), 283-299. Both the shipped row (input_row_index 880) and blind target 0 identify this exact same original article; the pairing flag (conflicting_dois) arose only because the shipped record uses the Wiley publisher DOI (10.1111/j.1467-8624.1966.tb05387.x) whereas the blind coding extracted the JSTOR DOI printed in the reference list (10.2307/1126804).

decisions.quote: We assessed memory performance and the presence or absence of verbalization behaviors of young children at different ages, and determined that the original pattern of findings was largely upheld: older children were more likely to verbalize, and their memory spans improved. We confirmed that 5- and 6-year-old children who verbalized recalled more than children who did not verbalize. However, unlike Flavell et al., substantial proportions of our 5- and 6-year-old samples overtly verbalized at least sometimes during the picture memory task. Also, continuous increase in overt verbalization from 7- to 10-years-old was not consistently evident in our samples.
decisions.reason: Both shipped and blind code the replication outcome for Flavell, Beach, and Chinsky (1966) as 'mixed'. While the authors report that the broad age-related increase in verbalization from age 5 to older children and the recall benefit of verbalization held, they qualify their overall conclusion ('largely upheld', 'replicated the spirit') and explicitly contrast several tested findings with the original study: unlike Flavell et al. (where 5-year-olds almost never verbalized), 76% of 5-year-olds verbalized at least sometimes, a continuous increase in speech from 7- to 10-year-olds was not confirmed, and the task order effect was reversed for all ages under 10.

decisions.quote: Specifically, this contemporary replication examined Flavell et al.’s findings in geographically diverse international samples to determine if the original findings are generalizable to modern data collection techniques (e.g. computerized task presentation).
decisions.reason: Both shipped and blind classify the study as a 'replication'. The authors collected new empirical data from 977 child participants across 17 laboratories following a modernized version of Flavell, Beach, and Chinsky's (1966) experimental protocol to re-test the original findings.
